piezas.titulo: Occupational Therapy in LGBTQ + Affirming Primary Care: Referral, Intervention, and Outcomes.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceLGBTQ + clients experience healthcare barriers that may shape daily routines, health management, and participation. Little is known about occupational therapy referral pathways and outcomes in LGBTQ + affirming primary care.ObjectiveTo describe referral characteristics, occupational performance concerns, intervention focus, and client-reported outcomes among LGBTQ + clients referred to occupational therapy.DesignRetrospective pilot program evaluation using clinical documentation and outcome data from July 2025 through March 2026, with a June 2026 analysis cutoff.SettingTwo Midwestern primary care settings where occupational therapy screening and referral processes were developed; ongoing intervention occurred through outpatient occupational therapy.ParticipantsThirty-nine referred clients were included in descriptive analyses; 38 received intervention beyond evaluation; 21 had complete baseline and follow-up Canadian Occupational Performance Measure data.InterventionIndividualized outpatient occupational therapy focused on client-identified concerns.Outcomes and MeasuresReferral and treatment characteristics, occupational performance concerns, coded occupational focus, and Canadian Occupational Performance Measure Performance and Satisfaction ratings.ResultsCommon concerns included instrumental activities of daily living (94.9%), health management/self-management (92.3%), activities of daily living (82.1%), and work or school participation (82.1%). The most common primary intervention focus was health management and chronic condition self-management (65.8%). Among participants with outcome data, COPM Performance scores improved by 2.29 points and Satisfaction scores improved by 2.58 points.Conclusions and RelevanceOccupational therapy may support LGBTQ + clients referred from primary care by addressing needs related to health management, routines, self-care, and participation through individualized outpatient intervention. Prospective multisite research is needed.

piezas.titulo: The psychometric applicability of the Chinese version of the childhood autism rating scale, second edition (CARS2) in Taiwanese autistic children.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Accurate assessment of autism characteristics is crucial for both clinical practice and research. Although several autism-related measures have been validated in Taiwan, the psychometric properties of the Chinese version of the Childhood Autism Rating Scale, Second Edition (CARS2) have not yet been fully evaluated. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the reliability and validity of the CARS2 in Taiwanese autistic children. Methods A total of 137 autistic children aged 3 to 12 years (mean = 6.32 ± 1.83 years) were assessed using either the CARS2 Standard Version (CARS2-ST) or High-Functioning Version (CARS2-HF), along with the Social Responsiveness Scale™, Second Edition (SRS™-2) and the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (VABS) First or Third Editions. Results The internal consistency for the CARS2-ST and CARS2-HF was good (α = 0.87 and 0.81, respectively). Convergent validity was supported by moderate to strong correlations between CARS2 scores and the SRS™-2 5-factor scores (r = 0.51-0.69, p Conclusions The findings support the use of the CARS2 as a culturally appropriate instrument with good internal consistency, construct validity, and responsiveness for assessing autism characteristics in Taiwanese children.

piezas.titulo: Psilocybin differentially shifts whole-brain network dynamics during information processing in autism
piezas.resumenOriginal: Autistic people process information differently, yet conventional analyses of brain activity during information processing shows few differences. However, how brain-wide intrinsic connectivity networks (ICNs) are engaged during processing is rarely considered, nor are the dynamics of brain states during tasks and their modulation by drugs such as psilocybin (which alters the activity of large-scale brain networks). Here, during shape- and face-matching, we confirmed no autistic/non-autistic differences in conventional task-dependent activity, but observed reduced default mode and salience network strength in autistic participants. Following 5 mg oral psilocybin we observed a differential effect of psilocybin between autistic and non-autistic participants characterised by a lower salience network strength in non-autistic participants but not in autistic participants. Our main analysis of ICN dynamics identified four transient brain states: face-processing, global-hypoactivity, salience-attention, and default-mode-executive networks. These states occurred in both groups under placebo and psilocybin conditions. However, in autistic participants, psilocybin shifted whole-brain dynamics away from salience-attention networks towards self-referential and task-execution networks, particularly during shape-matching. These findings demonstrate that psilocybin differentially modulates large-scale brain dynamics in autistic and non-autistic adults and provide a rationale to assess whether shifting brain dynamics during information processing with psilocybin has potential clinical benefits in autism.

piezas.titulo: Building an agentic stack in Envoy: routing models, tokens, and MCP
piezas.resumenOriginal: At Google Cloud, we believe the next generation of AI and agentic systems must be built on open, battle-tested foundations. Envoy, an open-source edge and service proxy designed for cloud-native applications, has already transformed microservices and modern cloud networking, powering everything from Google Cloud’s Application Load Balancers to the Agent Substrate dataplane on Google Kubernetes Engine. Now, Envoy is uniquely positioned to become the open standard for AI traffic, MCP tooling, and agent-to-agent communication. Earlier this year, we presented the technical case for Envoy networking in the agentic AI era , examining how autonomous AI agents fundamentally challenge traditional Layer 7 networking assumptions. Unlike microservices, autonomous agent workloads choose who they communicate with. In addition, their routing attributes live deep within request bodies, with their traffic governed by token budgets as well as request rates, and their multi-turn reasoning loops requiring stateful session affinity and strict tool execution boundaries. At Google Cloud, we have been working hard to develop Envoy for the agentic era. Read on for a closer look at how Envoy has evolved to better support autonomous agents, giving developers the performance and portability of an open-source ecosystem, backed by enterprise security and scalability. Why autonomous agents challenge traditional L7 proxies Over the past decade, Envoy became the industry standard for cloud-native traffic management by operating cleanly at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP connection management) and Layer 7 (URI, method, and header-based routing). Autonomous agents introduce two higher-order protocol layers: Layer 8 (agentic interaction protocols): such as LLM APIs , Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) , running over JSON-RPC 2.0 or gRPC. Critical policy attributes—such as tools/call , tool_name: "execute_sql" , or model: "gemini-1.5-pro" —are serialized inside the request payload. Layer 9 (agent framework interfaces): Coordination frameworks such as UCP, AP2, and Google Cloud’s Agent Development Kit, where multi-turn workflows produce dynamic token consumption and non-linear execution graphs. Fronting these workloads with traditional L7 proxies creates four major architectural challenges: Payload blindness: Nearly all LLM traffic shares the same paths (such as /v1/chat/completions ), so a header-based proxy cannot distinguish between a low-cost query and an expensive 500,000-token prompt, or one model from another. Request rate limiting fallacy: One request per minute with a massive context window can use more accelerator compute and memory bandwidth than dozens of short queries, and agent loops can burn through budgets unnoticed. Stateless load balancing: Each turn of an agent's conversation should go back to the server that already remembers it. Traditional load balancers send it to whichever server is next, so the model has to start over for every turn, this wastes time and GPUs. Ungoverned tool execution: Agents query databases, execute code in sandboxes, and call third-party APIs. Without inline inspection of MCP tool calls, organizations risk prompt injection, data exfiltration, and runaway billing loops. The core pillars of Envoy’s agentic stack To address these challenges, Envoy provides capabilities that turn the network into an active governance layer: Core Pillar Operational Functionality 1. Native body parser Payload blindness: Read request bodies, not just headers. Line-rate payload normalization across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini schemas with SSE stream handling. 2. Tokenomics engine Request-rate fallacy: Count tokens, not just requests. Pre-inference token estimation, tokens per minute (TPM) / tokens per day (TPD) rate limiting 3. Model & MCP routing Stateless load balancing: Keep agent sessions on the right servers Endpoint Picker (EPP) model dispatch, KV-cache prefix affinity, MCP Stateless support. 4. AI security guardrails Ungoverned tool execution: Policy tool calls. Inline policy, decision point (ext_proc) callouts for guardrails: Model Armor, ShieldGemma, and data loss prevention. 1. Native wire-format body parsing and transcoding Client applications often get locked into specific model APIs. For example, client code built for OpenAI's schema cannot communicate with Anthropic's endpoints or Google’s Gemini without client-side translation layers. To help, Envoy ecosystem includes native body parsers that normalize requests across diverse model families, providing: Client abstraction: Upstream applications send a standardized schema. Envoy inspects the JSON payload at line-rate, extracts the target model, and dynamically transcodes the request into the downstream provider's native format. No application code changes: Switching from an external commercial model to a self-hosted open-source model (such as Gemma or Llama on vLLM) requires only an Envoy configuration update. Application code remains unchanged. Streaming token extraction: Envoy parses server-sent events (SSE) response streams in real time, capturing token counts from usage chunks while maintaining ultra-low time-to-first-token latency. 2. Tokenomics engine: token-aware traffic management In AI networking, tokens are the fundamental unit of capacity . Envoy replaces coarse request counters with token-aware traffic management features such as: Token rate limiting: Enforces tokens per minute (TPM) and tokens per day (TPD) limits per tenant, project, or model. Pre-inference throttling: Envoy estimates input tokens from request payload bytes and extracts actual token usage from LLM responses to record in a quota database, rejecting subsequent over-quota requests with an HTTP 429 before they reach the inference cluster. Runaway loop protection: Autonomous agents can enter recursive reasoning loops. By tracking cumulative token consumption and message counts per session or agent ID, Envoy throttles multi-turn sessions once an agent exceeds its assigned budget. 3. Model routing and Model Context Protocol (MCP) support Envoy manages traffic for both downstream model backends and outbound tool calls, with: KV-cache prefix affinity: Using the Kubernetes Gateway API Inference Extensions and Endpoint Picker (EPP), Envoy routes prompts sharing identical system instructions to the GPU worker currently holding that cache in memory, reducing latency. Model retry and fallback: If a primary model returns a 429 status code or fails, Envoy automatically retries or redirects the request to a secondary model pool with zero client interruption. MCP tool routing: For MCP agents, Envoy routes requests via JSON-RPC 2.0 bodies and HTTP headers. Per the 2026-07-28 MCP specification , Envoy uses Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers for zero-body-parsing routing to backend servers. Backends reject header-body mismatches with an HTTP 400 / -32020 (HeaderMismatch) error to prevent tampering. 4. AI security guardrails Inline safety filtering cannot come at the expense of network throughput. To prevent this, Envoy provides security callouts: Using standardized external processing ( ext_proc ), Envoy connects to dedicated policy decision engines — such as Google Cloud’s Model Armor, ShieldGemma, or local classifiers — to detect prompt injections and sensitive data leaks with minimal latency overhead. High-density infrastructure: Envoy and Agent Substrate In enterprise production environments, agents frequently spend time idle between user queries or long-running tool executions. Running hundreds of thousands of idle agents in dedicated containers or virtual machines can create prohibitive infrastructure costs. Envoy pairs directly with high-density execution runtimes like Agent Substrate to provide: Scale-to-zero traffic steering: Agent Substrate uses lightweight isolation runtimes (such as Cloud Hypervisor, microVMs and gVisor application sandboxes) that can suspend and resume in milliseconds. When traffic arrives for a suspended agent, Envoy buffers the initial packet while signaling the runtime to resume the instance, completing the end-to-end resume in milliseconds. Egress perimeter defense: Envoy functions as both an ingress and egress gateway for agent environments, routing the inbound traffic and restricting outbound network calls to verified domains and preventing untrusted autonomous code from reaching unauthorized endpoints. Getting started Envoy has evolved into an intelligent, extensible networking layer designed specifically for the unique demands of multi-agent architectures. To begin building with the agentic stack in Envoy: Explore the code: Review the Envoy proxy and Agent Router implementations on Github and examine the open-source sample configurations. Join the community: Participate in CNCF, Gateway API , and Kubernetes AI Gateway Working Group to collaborate on standardized inference APIs, MCP routing specifications, and token management conventions.

piezas.resumenOriginal: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense STAR Admin Fri, 02/17/2023 - 20:50 Join STAR Institute and some of its expert clinicians for three nights of learning as we explore the keys to a sensory-informed life. Each night, STAR's Clinical Director will be joined by a different STAR therapist to share tips and strategies around some of families' most often asked questions including: “How can I support and be there for my family when I am constantly feeling burned out?” “What can I do to help my child transition from thing to thing/place to place more smoothly?" “We feel like we walk on egg shells around our child. Why is that and what can we do?" Each night will begin with a 30-40 minute conversation led by the therapist before a live Q&A where you can ask STAR’s occupational therapists and mental health providers your own questions. Discussions You Don't Want to Miss: Caring for Yourself So You Can Care for Others Keys to Successful Transitions in Life’s Big and Small Moments Beyond Fight, Flight, or Freeze: How to Support Regulation STAR Voices You'll Hear From: Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L (she/her) Clinical Director Mim Ochsenbein, MSW, OTR/L has been a practicing pediatric occupational therapist for over 25 years. She received her BSc in Occupational Therapy from the University of Southern California (USC) in 1996 and her MSW from the University of California-Los Angeles (UCLA) in 2012. She has received advanced training in sensory integration (SIPT certification, STAR ProCert1, STAR ProCert2), listening therapy (Therapeutic Listening, iLs), feeding therapy (SOS), DIR, mental health (DC:0-5 Diagnostic Classification of Mental Health Disorders of Infancy and Early Childhood), and infant massage (CIMI). Her work in occupational therapy with children and youth has occurred in a variety of settings including early intervention, school based, clinic based, mental health and private practice. As a social worker, she provided case management, program development, and program management. Mim has taught both university level (California State-Dominguez Hills) and professional continuing education courses since 2013, spoken internationally, and has co-authored works for professional publications. She has been in her current role at STAR Institute since 2017 at the invitation of Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, PhD, FAOTA, OTR. Gina Crites, OTR/L, MFTC Counselor Gina has a Master’s degree in Marriage and Family Therapy from the University of New Hampshire (2009). She currently provides therapy to individuals (8 years through adulthood), couples, and families in-person or through telehealth (Colorado residents only). Clients would describe Gina’s style as reflective, collaborative, and experiential. She has a calm yet dynamic presence and works from a compassionate, curious, and empowering stance. Gina’s practice is rooted in attachment and systems theories, making her truly a relationally focused therapist. As such, she believes that our greatest healing occurs in the context of relationships. She has always been oriented toward a biopsychosocial approach to her theory of change, thereby honoring the importance of the mind-body connection. She believes that within a safe space and through our attuned relationship with Self and others, we all have the power to tune into our instinct towards healing. With her early career in occupational therapy, Gina has incredible understanding of the importance of self-determination for clients: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. This—coupled with her deep understanding of sensory integration and processing and the importance of occupational roles—truly sets her apart. Her practice honors and respects each person’s unique history and individual differences, and sets clients up for experiencing a deeper sense of self and relational health, on the clients’ own terms. Gina was drawn to couples and family therapy for its non-pathologizing approach to viewing clients’ problems. While biological factors certainly play a role, so do clients’ experiences within their families, partnerships, and larger society. She is passionate about empowering parents to reflect on and integrate their own experiences in service of their children’s health and wellness, as well as their own. “Society does not prioritize proactively supporting its members’ health and therefore, parents and families are not set up for success. This is particularly true for oppressed groups, the poorly included and the disenfranchised.” She believes that parents innately know how high the stakes are and are doing their best, and, like all of us, only benefit from being and feeling less alone in their pain and struggle. Gina is especially equipped to support neurodivergent individuals, couples and families, as well as those navigating issues around disability and chronic illness. She is capable of easily moving between deep therapeutic work, parent coaching and individual skills training - making her a versatile therapist. She has experience supporting clients with life transitions, anxiety, depression, non-suicidal self-harm, suicidal ideation, recovery from adverse childhood experiences and trauma, developing deeper emotional awareness, identifying and leaving behind maladaptive coping patterns, and improving self-esteem. Above all, Gina is a sensory informed, neurodiversity affirming and LGBTQIA+ allied, culturally sensitive and attachment-focused therapist with a special interest in interpersonal neurobiology who strongly believes in the healing power of making sense of our experiences in the context of relationships where we feel seen, heard, and understood. She then completed a doctorate in occupational therapy at Creighton University. Jayna was the first Occupational Therapy Pediatric Resident (now called Fellowship) with Creighton University following her occupational therapy degree. During this time, she received advanced training in Sensory Integration and Processing, feeding, the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit, and education. Jayna has worked in a variety of pediatric settings prior to coming to STAR Institute and is Board Certified in Pediatrics through the American Occupational Therapy Association (AOTA). Jayna is an ally to the neurodiverse community and strives to learn more and integrate practices which support neurodiverse persons to build a strong sense of self and live their most sensory-rich lives. piezas.titulo: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
piezas.resumenOriginal: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job. At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context. Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s Hospital Occupation: Clinical AI Engineer Education: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job . When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein , chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s. Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?” For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says. Between medicine and engineering Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists. For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients. His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces , a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use. That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year. At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job. Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers” One project, called clinical doppelgangers , is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies. The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance. Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong. Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome. Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems. Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them. Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection. “That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.” After the prompt In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake? That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says. Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use . “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.” An evolving career The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter . Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms. What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down. That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles. “The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

piezas.titulo: Fragments: November 10
piezas.resumenOriginal: It’s that time of the year when the November Thoughtworks Technology Radar appears. Again my colleagues have taken a sweep of the technologies that our teams have used in the field, and pulled together a summary of what’s popped up in the last six months. It’s been a busy half-year, one that again has been dominated by AI, and that’s reflected in the many AI blips on the radar. The mass of blips makes it hard to develop a coherent story around trends, but Chris Ford has done a fine job of the writing the accompanying article on macro trends . One team of passionate people experimenting with agents can make almost anything work. They share a context, a credit card and a mental model. They review each other’s work because they sit together, and they know what to check and how much latitude to give the coding agent. Two hundred people, though, cannot work that way. The moment agentic AI becomes an operating model rather than a pilot, a second layer of problems appears: How is context shared between teams? What’s the token bill? How do we deal with increased review demands? What’s the agent allowed to reach, read and change? And who’s now responsible for the harness everyone depends on? Experience so far suggests that the questions that enterprises face are about: shared context, token cost, cognitive load, security, and platform building. While these issues are distinct, they are not separate, so strategies to answer them must take all of them into account. I also echo Chris in reminding us that however impressive these tools are, we must remember that while we have to rethink systems and workflows to utilize these technologies, they should be built to serve humans - and we should all benefit from its bounty. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Ben Thompson’s Stratechery newsletter reflects on the recent election’s impact on data centers . I watch a lot of sports, and particularly this fall, watched a lot of baseball. My Milwaukee Brewers — excuse me, my World Champion Milwaukee Brewers — demanded my full attention, which also meant I saw a lot of campaign ads, and by far the most common topic, at least here in Wisconsin, was data centers. Moreover, it was never entirely clear which way it cut politically: both parties were anti-data center, accusing their opponent of being the opposite. He points out that this opposition is recent, and tied to a shift in focus from the internet and streaming movies to AI: you know, the technology that in the best case scenario is going to take everyone’s jobs, and in the worst case scenario end the human race. There’s going to be a lot said about how Democratic officials will be at the heart of blocking data center building, but as his point above about campaign ads illustrates, the opposition to data centers is (at least at the moment) a bi-partisan opposition. He follows up with “ten takes” from these consequences. The big beneficiaries of this opposition to building data centers will be those who own the data centers that have already been built. The opposition will reduce supply of tokens, meaning that token costs will go up, thus increasing the profits for those who already have their token generators plugged in and humming. There’s also benefits to those who aren’t constrained by the need to build more big data centers. Other countries aren’t affected by a change in US policy, China is the most talked-about case here, but it’s not the only country that may benefit from a drop in US data center building. Apple may also benefit, if it means more AI work is pushed to edge devices that are their territory, in addition to having not sunk so many dollars into AI-specific investments. To his analysis, I’ll add that this may also have a somewhat counter-intuitive effect on regulation, and corporate attitudes to it. The common expectation is that businesses are opposed to government regulation, since that interferes with their free pursuit of profit. That’s true to an extent, but it’s quite common to see established businesses lobby (quietly) in favor of regulation that acts as a barrier to new competitors. So I wouldn’t be at all surprised to see companies that have already built data centers to be pushing for regulations that impede or prevent new ones from being built. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve been a long-time fan of Hadley Wickham, for how he has tamed the rather messy world of R programming into a well-designed tidyverse . He is another thoughtful voice to listen to as we move into the world of agentic engineering , in this case by trying to figure out what the real cost of tokens is . I hear a lot of suspicion that AI tokens are unsustainably priced and that frontier labs are heavily subsidising costs with their VC money. They want to get us hooked now, so they can pull the rug out from under us whenever they want to make a bunch of money. Is that true? My sense is that it’s mostly not. But can I back that up with some data? His conclusion is that it doesn’t seem that token costs are significantly subsidized on per-token API basis, but they are with subscription plans. (He caveats his analysis, saying it doesn’t take into account recouping the costs of training the models.) ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ There’s a creepy excitement at the thought that models are clever enough to edit the weights of models, an activity that Takehi et al refer to as Weight-Space Programming . Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. While we don’t know if we’ll ever be able to download skills directly into our brains ( “I know kung fu” - or for those in my particular demographic: Joe 90 ), this does raise the possibility of downloading capabilities into models by manipulating their weights. Simon Wilison riffed on this paper by examining whether an LLM can understand model behaviors from the weights alone , by examining four simple neural networks, each trained to play a specific game, and figuring out which game it was by just looking at the weights. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Jessica Kerr (jessitron): My days of teaching AI to do stuff are numbered. Getting it to teach me stuff is more fun. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Houck et al (that “al” includes some folks who I’ve learned to pay a lot of attention to), look at how we can assess the quality of context supplied to agents. An agent may draw from source code, specifications, issue trackers, chat histories, architectural documents, tool output, and user instructions, then act on that combination with limited human supervision. Information that was written for different audiences, at different times, and for different purposes is brought together into a temporary operating environment for a particular task. Whether each source is individually useful does not reveal whether the resulting context is fit for the work the agent is being asked to do. They’ve come up with a framework for describing the quality of this assembled context , which they refer to as CAFE(S). The acronym refers to five dimensions they look at: Clarity: Can the agent interpret the request as intended? Actionability: Can the agent proceed, and know when it is done? Fidelity: Can the agent trust that this context is true? Efficiency: Can the agent focus on what matters? Security: Should the agent have this context at all? They also list a set of half-a-dozen “context smells”: common cases where these break down (and a nod to Kent’s original metaphor ) I’m not sure about the name, (how exactly should I pronounce “CAFE(S)”?) and the article exhibits rather more LLM Voice that I prefer. But on the whole I think this is a good framing for thinking about an important part of feeding our silicon servants/overlords. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Cindy Sridharan noted that the problems she ran into six months ago are no longer around : What was missing in my setup 6 months ago was the verification process I now use. 70% of my daily token spend goes into verifying patches, and only ~20-30% into creating them. That resonated with conversations I’ve had with folks using agents in enterprise settings. They are using far more tokens to check the working of models (through guardrails and evals) than they are to generate a response to a request. A single request to a model from a customer may trigger a dozen turns to other models to probe its input and verify its output.

piezas.titulo: Why Your RAG Pipeline, Not Your LLM, Is Causing Hallucinations
piezas.resumenOriginal: Every time a large language model produces a confidently wrong answer, the industry reaches for the same word: hallucination. It’s a tidy label. It frames the failure as a mysterious, almost biological quirk of the model itself, as if the AI briefly lost touch with reality and there’s not much anyone can do about it except wait for a better model. That framing is convenient for model vendors. It is much less convenient for the truth. In production systems, especially retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, which is how most enterprise AI actually gets deployed the majority of “hallucinations” I’ve seen traced back to something far less mysterious: bad data engineering. Stale indexes. Naive chunking. Missing metadata. Broken retrieval ranking. Silent ingestion failures. None of that is a model problem. All of it gets blamed on the model anyway. If you work in data engineering and you’ve been treating hallucination as someone else’s problem a model-layer issue for the ML team to solve it’s worth looking closer. There’s a good chance the fix lives in your pipeline, not their weights.

piezas.titulo: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer
piezas.resumenOriginal: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. This allows the model to apply more reasoning and reach the right answer with fewer tokens, especially on tasks such as agentic coding that depend on reasoning quality. GLM 5.4 is not yet available as open weights: We plan to open-source the model weights responsibly after completing necessary safety hardening. I tried it out using the Z.ai API, for which I had to sign up for their Coding Plan subscription because 5.4 cannot currently be accessed through the regular API. It turns out both coding plan and regular API share the same OpenAI-compatible Responses API (at https://api.z.ai/api/v1 ), and the API key for the coding plan worked with that and gave me access to the new model. I built a llm-glm plugin , then realized that llm-zai by Tommy Hughes already exists! I've shipped mine purely because llm-zai doesn't yet support the new model, but I'll likely retire mine once that plugin catches up. Here are pelicans for GLM-5.4 on low, high, and max. This is the max one: I realized I never ran pelicans for GLM-5.3, so here those are for the same effort levels. They look similar in quality to 5.4. It's interesting how GLM 5.1 and GLM 5.2 produced radically different pelicans from other models. The pelicans for 5.3 and 5.4 are much more comparable to those I get from OpenAI or Anthropic models - the previous generations had their own distinctive look. I made a comparison grid showing the four generations of GLM pelicans all in one place. The style transition between 5.2 and 5.3 is pretty stark. piezas.titulo: Comparative effectiveness, clinical importance, and certainty of acupuncture-based therapies for post-stroke depression: a systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo compare the relative effectiveness of acupuncture and acupuncture-based combination therapies for post-stroke depression (PSD) and to assess the certainty of evidence for the key outcomes.MethodsSix databases were searched from inception to March 1, 2026. Random-effects network meta-analyses compared eight treatment strategies for depressive symptoms, neurological impairment, and activities of daily living. HAMD results were synthesized as standardized mean differences (SMDs) to accommodate different scale versions; SDS, NIHSS, and MBI results were expressed as mean differences. Clinical interpretation considered confidence intervals, outcome-specific reference benchmarks where applicable, and CINeMA certainty ratings. A common three-point HAMD threshold was not applied across versions.ResultsWe included 125 randomized controlled trials involving 10,251 participants. ACU-rTMS had the highest HAMD ranking and was associated with lower scores than antidepressants (SMD, −2.17; 95% CI, −3.63 to −0.70) and standard care (SMD, −3.30; 95% CI, −4.86 to −1.74), with moderate-certainty evidence. Its comparison with rTMS remained uncertain (SMD, −1.17; 95% CI, −2.35 to 0.01; low certainty). A validated common HAMD threshold for clinical importance was unavailable. SDS and functional outcomes suggested potential benefits, but confidence intervals frequently included effects below the reference benchmarks. Of 86 network comparisons, none had high-certainty evidence. Comparative safety could not be established.ConclusionAcupuncture-based therapies may improve selected outcomes in PSD. ACU-rTMS is promising, but its incremental benefit over rTMS and the clinical importance of its standardized HAMD effects remain uncertain. Heterogeneity, possible measurement and small-study biases, predominantly middle-aged and older Chinese populations, and limited safety and long-term data restrict clinical recommendations.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261465363.

piezas.titulo: A neuro-computational framework for modeling developmental changes in cross-sensory interactions in autism
piezas.resumenOriginal: Recent studies have shown that multisensory processing in children shifts from a competitive to a facilitative state as development progresses, and this transition appears delayed in children with autism spectrum diagnosis (ASD). The neural mechanisms underlying this developmental change, and its alteration in ASD, remain largely unknown. To address this gap, we investigated how sensory modalities interact in the developing brain using a biologically plausible neuro-computational model governed by Hebbian learning rules. We also explored the neural substrates that may underlie atypical multisensory development in ASD. Our results suggest that the net effective influence of cross-modal interactions gradually shifts from suppressive to facilitatory during development, mediating the observed shift from competition to facilitation in typical children. Furthermore, our simulations show that the delayed transition in ASD may stem either from reduced neural plasticity or diminished multisensory experience. Our model provides a computational framework for examining how differences in multisensory experience and in the rate of synaptic weight updating may shape the developmental trajectory of cross-modal interactions. By linking computational modeling with behavioral findings, our work provides a framework for understanding atypical sensory development.

piezas.titulo: Frequency-specific cortical swallowing-network responses following neuroengineering-guided individualized multichannel tDCS.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background Neuromodulatory interventions for dysphagia are increasingly explored as adjunctive rehabilitation strategies, yet their efficacy may be limited by non-individualized stimulation protocols and insufficient consideration of network-specific brain dynamics. Advances in neuroengineering now enable individualized targeting based on functional neuroimaging and computational modeling, offering the potential for precision neuromodulation of swallowing-related brain networks. Methods We investigated whether individualized multichannel transcranial direct current stimulation (mc-tDCS), optimized using magnetoencephalography (MEG)-derived target localization, MRI-based finite-element head modeling, and a distributed constrained maximum intensity (D-CMI) optimization framework, modulates the cortical swallowing network. In a randomized sham-controlled crossover design, eight healthy adults underwent three stimulation conditions: low-intensity mc-tDCS (1.5 mA), high-intensity mc-tDCS (4.0 mA), and sham stimulation. Swallowing-related cortical activity was assessed before and after stimulation using MEG source reconstruction of event-related desynchronization during uncued voluntary swallowing and a visually cued swallowing task requiring precise timing. A repeated-measures Dose × Task × Time model tested the hypothesized interaction separately in five frequency bands, with Holm correction across bands. Results No Dose × Task × Time interaction was significant after Holm correction across the five frequency bands (all adjusted p ≥ 0.274). Within-condition pre-post analyses identified alpha- and beta-band changes after 1.5-mA stimulation during challenged swallowing and a low-gamma change after 4.0-mA stimulation during uncued swallowing. Challenged-task timing accuracy increased over time, without significant Dose or Dose × Time effects. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of integrating individualized MEG-based targeting, subject-specific head modeling, and optimized multichannel stimulation. The hypothesized Dose × Task × Time interaction was not significant. Exploratory within-condition pre-post differences were observed in alpha, beta, and low-gamma activity, but do not establish stimulation-specific effects. Larger controlled studies are needed to evaluate the physiological effects of this individualized approach.

piezas.titulo: Ascending somatosensory systems processing affiliative social touch.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Affiliative social touch is a fundamental channel of mammalian communication that influences attachment, parenting, social buffering, play, and reproduction. Traditionally, somatosensory research focused on discriminative properties of touch, while later studies emphasized affective touch mediated by C-tactile afferents and related pathways. Here, we propose a broader framework in which affiliative social touch is understood not as a specialized affective modality but as a multidimensional social signal whose meaning depends on context, internal state, social relationship, and behavioral goals. Drawing primarily on rodent models, we review the ascending somatosensory systems that convey affiliative tactile information from the periphery to the brain. We discuss the contributions of low-threshold mechanoreceptors, the vibrissal system, and also spinal circuits that begin transforming tactile signals into affectively relevant representations. We further examine parallel ascending pathways through the brainstem, thalamus, and cortex, highlighting the roles of the parabrachial nucleus, posterior intralaminar thalamic nucleus, hypothalamic and limbic networks, and cortical systems involved in sensory processing, salience detection, and social cognition. Neuromodulatory systems, including oxytocin, endogenous opioids, dopamine, and serotonin, which shape the behavioral interpretation of affiliative social touch are also discussed. Finally, we consider the conservation of these mechanisms in human. The paper argues that affiliative social touch is not encoded by dedicated pathways for specific social behaviors; rather, common somatosensory signals gain social meaning through interactions with distributed neural circuits and state-dependent modulatory mechanisms. Understanding how ascending somatosensory pathways transform affiliative social contact into socially meaningful representations provides a unifying framework for investigating the neural basis of social behavior.

piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Ana-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana (Italia) Presentador: Paolo Rosso, Universidad Politécnica de Valencia (España). Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: Scaling massive AI/ML workloads with IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine clusters
piezas.resumenOriginal:
TL;DR: Single-stack IPv6 on GKE runs both nodes and pods without having to use private IPv4 addresses. Available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, it works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Long before they run out of compute or power, AI applications hit another wall: running out of IP addresses. A single AI deployment often requires a vast address space to support everything from thousands of accelerator nodes, scaling inference replicas, bursting Ray workers and pipelines, pod sidecars, and services like vector databases. Running a dual stack — IPv6 behind a private IPv4 space — can help, but only to a point, because the private IPv4 space has often already been exhausted across existing networks. To help, today, we're announcing single-stack IPv6 on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), allowing you to run both nodes and pods on IPv6, without private IPv4 addresses. Single-stack IPv6 is available in preview for Cloud TPU v6e and CPU node pools, including Axion, and works with DNS64/NAT64 to reach IPv4 endpoints. Nodes and pods run IPv6-only across Cloud TPU v6e and CPU-based node pools, with no private IPv4. Workloads reach Google Cloud APIs over native IPv6 and IPv4-only endpoints through DNS64/NAT64. What single-stack IPv6 delivers The availability of single-stack IPv6 in GKE is a game-changer for large AI deployments. Consider the following features and benefits that it brings to the table: 1. No private IPv4 required for nodes or pods Nodes and pods use IPv6 exclusively. Without the RFC 1918 footprint that governs private IPv4 address spaces, clusters avoid conflicts with on-premises networks, peered VPCs, or adjacent clusters. 2. IPv4 interoperability with DNS64/NAT64 You enable DNS64 on the VPC, and NAT64 on a regional Cloud NAT gateway, allowing pods to transparently reach IPv4-only endpoints, registries, and dataset hubs — refer to the documentation to learn how to configure DNS64 and set up Cloud NAT . 3. Massive address space per node Each node receives a /112 pod range (65,536 addresses), so IP address capacity no longer limits how high your clusters, nodes, or pods can scale. Standard GKE maximum-pods-per-node limits still apply. 4. Broad accelerator and compute support We designed single-stack IPv6 in GKE with the goal of supporting a range of accelerators and general compute families. At preview, it supports Cloud TPU v6e (Trillium), plus E2, N1, N2, N2D, N4, C3, C3D, C4, C4D, C4A, and Z3 machine families, with support for additional accelerators and machine families coming soon. 5. Direct workload observability Every pod has a unique IPv6 address without having to run NAT inside the cluster, simplifying telemetry, network policies, and debugging. Performance and scale Single-stack IPv6 removes private IPv4 address limits without additional data plane overhead. In our internal testing, we saw the following performance characteristics: Pod lifecycle: Burst pod scheduling and CNI sandbox setup performed at parity with IPv4. Networking : Inter-node TCP/UDP latency and multi-stream pod-to-pod throughput matched IPv4. Services and DNS : eBPF service load balancing and NodeLocalDNS showed no measurable overhead compared to standard IPv4. Start building today Single-stack IPv6 is available now in preview on GKE version 1.37.1-gke.3020000 To create your first IPv6-only cluster, run the following commands, replacing REGION and CLUSTER_NAME: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# 1. Create a VPC with internal (ULA) IPv6 enabled
gcloud compute networks create gke-ipv6-net \
 --subnet-mode=custom \
 --enable-ula-internal-ipv6

# 2. Enable DNS64 for the VPC
gcloud dns policies create gke-ipv6-dns64 \
 --networks=gke-ipv6-net \
 --enable-dns64-all-queries

# 3. Enable NAT64 in your region
gcloud compute routers create gke-ipv6-router \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net --region=REGION
gcloud compute routers nats create gke-ipv6-nat64 \
 --router=gke-ipv6-router --region=REGION \
 --auto-allocate-nat-external-ips \
 --nat64-all-v6-subnet-ip-ranges

# 4. Create the cluster
gcloud beta container clusters create CLUSTER_NAME \
 --cluster-version=1.37.1-gke.3020000 \
 --location=REGION \
 --enable-dataplane-v2 \
 --cluster-dns=clouddns \
 --stack-type=ipv6 \
 --network=gke-ipv6-net \
 --create-subnetwork name=my-subnet \
 --ipv6-access-type=internal'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5e2ef96190>)])]> To learn more, see the documentation .

piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: Task-specific sensorimotor rhythm dynamics during action observation in chronic stroke and healthy adults
piezas.resumenOriginal: Action Observation Therapy (AOT) is used in rehabilitation research because observing goal-directed actions may engage neural processes relevant to motor learning after stroke. However, the neurophysiological responses elicited by different types of observed actions, and their temporal evolution, remain incompletely understood. Previous EEG work showed that goal-directed activities of daily living, particularly the reaching phases of feeding and self-care actions, elicit stronger sensorimotor rhythm suppression in chronic stroke survivors. We therefore investigated task-specific rhythm modulation during observation of activities of daily living in healthy participants and individuals with chronic stroke. Twenty stroke survivors with right hemiparesis (≥6 months post-stroke) and 23 healthy controls were included. Participants observed standardized videos of finalized and non-finalized actions, as well as control videos. EEG Event-Related Spectral Perturbation analysis was used to assess power changes in the α-(8–13 Hz) and β-band (14–25 Hz) bands across temporal intervals and action categories. Linear mixed-effects models examined within- and between-group effects. Both groups exhibited greater reactivity at central scalp sites during finalized actions than during control videos. Healthy participants showed earlier and more pronounced β-band desynchronization. Individuals with stroke showed delayed and weaker β-band suppression, particularly over the affected hemisphere, while retaining responses to goal-directed actions. The main between-group β-band differences persisted after adjustment for age. During feeding actions, stroke participants showed a lower β-desynchronization peak frequency at C3 than healthy controls (15.3 vs. 17.5 Hz), remaining significant after age adjustment (p = 0.003) and correction for multiple comparisons. Self-care and feeding actions were associated with more sustained modulation, whereas external and non-finalized actions showed earlier rebound patterns, particularly in healthy participants. These findings indicate that goal-directed activities of daily living are associated with distinct temporal patterns of baseline-referenced oscillatory activity and support further evaluation of task-specific stimuli in future AOT studies. The EEG findings should not be interpreted as direct or specific evidence of mirror-neuron-system activation or as evidence of treatment efficacy.
